title: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition) · Units 27–28
description: Internet research, digital safety, academic study, assessment and educational communication through natural English collocations.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied book. Target phrases are based on the teaching pages, practice material and answer key; all translations, usage notes and full teaching example sentences are newly written. Original exercise prompts, passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, exercise pages, page illustrations and relevant answer-key entries checked for both units; significant learning targets and contextual corrections retained.

units.title: Unit 27 — Using the Internet
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 58–59 (PDF pages 62–63).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Work and study · internet research and digital safety
learningObjectives: Research a topic online using keywords, effective searches and critical assessment of information sources.
Record and reference web sources correctly without copying another author’s prose.
Distinguish downloading, uploading, making backups and accessing cloud storage.
Use accurate verb patterns to discuss malware, spam, attachments, links and computer failures.

items.example: Before researching a topic, make a note of keywords that describe it.
items.note: Make a note of means write something down so you can use it later; do a note is not idiomatic.

items.example: You can do a web search to find introductory articles on the subject.
items.note: Do combines with web search; web search means looking for information online.

items.example: The library recommends several online resources for language learners.
items.note: Resources here means useful sources of information or learning materials accessed online.

items.example: A search engine can help you find academic websites.
items.note: A search engine is a tool for finding online information through search terms.

items.example: The university website offers hints and tips for new students.
items.note: This paired expression means practical advice; it often appears in guides and help pages.

items.example: If the results are too broad, refine your search with a more specific phrase.
items.note: Refine a search means make it more precise, often by adjusting keywords or filters.

items.example: Students should evaluate sites critically before quoting their information.
items.note: Critically means carefully examining the reliability and quality of a source, not merely criticising it.

items.example: Researchers sometimes subscribe to online journals for specialist articles.
items.note: Subscribe to means arrange regular access, which may be paid or free.

items.example: The archive lets you search by keyword or publication date.
items.note: By keyword indicates the method used to search a database or archive.

items.example: You can find older interviews in the magazine's back issues.
items.note: Back issues are earlier published editions, not technical problems or delays.

items.example: I often copy and paste a link into my notes for later reading.
items.note: A fixed computing expression; copying someone else's prose into an essay without attribution is not acceptable.

items.example: Explain the idea in your own words instead of repeating the article.
items.note: Used when paraphrasing or explaining an idea independently.

items.word: keep a record of the source
items.example: Always keep a record of the source when collecting material for a report.
items.note: Keep a record of means preserve details so they can be checked or cited later.

items.example: Students must reference a source correctly in their essays.
items.note: Reference is a verb here meaning provide proper bibliographic acknowledgement.

items.example: We use the Internet for research before writing our project reports.
items.note: For research expresses purpose; the Internet is the medium, not necessarily a reliable source by itself.

items.pt: ler atentamente os resultados da busca
items.example: Read through search results carefully before selecting sources for your report.
items.note: Read through suggests examining multiple search results, not merely running the search.

items.example: You should install anti-virus software before using the new computer.
items.note: Install is the conventional verb for putting software onto a device; antivirus is also commonly written as one word.

items.example: Regular updates can help protect your computer from viruses.
items.note: Protect something from something identifies the threat being prevented.

items.example: Our email provider uses filters to block spam.
items.note: Spam means unsolicited messages; block spam is the normal verb–noun pairing.

items.example: Remember to update your anti-virus program when a new version is available.
items.note: Update means install current fixes or protection data; do not confuse it with install.

items.example: Do not click on a link from an unknown sender.
items.note: Click on is the conventional preposition pattern for selecting a link.

items.example: I couldn't open an attachment because the file was damaged.
items.note: Attachment refers to a file sent with a message; open is the ordinary verb.

items.example: You can download an application from the developer's official site.
items.note: Download means transfer data from a remote source to your device; contrast upload.

items.example: A suspicious file may contain malware that steals information.
items.note: Malware is malicious software; contain describes what is inside a file or programme.

items.example: Someone tried to hack into a computer in the university network.
items.note: Hack into means gain unauthorised access; the preposition into is important.

items.example: Criminals may try to steal personal information through fake websites.
items.note: Steal combines with data and information when it is obtained dishonestly.

items.pt: fazer cópia de segurança dos seus arquivos
items.example: Before updating the operating system, back up your files.
items.note: Back up is a separable phrasal verb meaning create a safety copy; the noun is backup.

items.pt: enviar seus arquivos para um serviço on-line
items.example: You can upload your files to the course platform before the deadline.
items.note: Upload means send data from your device to an online service; contrast download.

items.example: We use cloud storage to share documents across the team.
items.note: Cloud storage means storing files on remotely accessible systems rather than only on a local device.

items.pt: um sistema de armazenamento em nuvem
items.example: The team uses a cloud storage system for project backups.
items.note: A countable phrase referring to a service or system for storing files online.

items.pt: um pen drive; dispositivo de memória USB
items.example: She saved her slides on a memory stick before the conference.
items.note: In British English, a memory stick is a small removable USB storage device; USB stick is another name.

items.pt: um computador trava; um computador deixa de funcionar
items.example: If a computer crashes during a test, report the problem to the supervisor.
items.note: Crash means stop working unexpectedly, often causing work to be lost.

items.example: Without a backup, you could lose your files after a disk failure.
items.note: Lose combines naturally with files, data and work; it does not necessarily imply theft.

items.example: To reduce security problems, update software regularly.
items.note: Regularly modifies how often updates are made; it does not guarantee complete security.

items.pt: pesquisar em um banco de dados por palavra-chave
items.example: You can search a database by keyword to locate recent studies.
items.note: A specific search-by-keyword pattern confirmed by the exercise and answer key.

items.example: We had to search through back issues of the journal for the original article.
items.note: Through indicates examining a set of earlier publications.

items.word: make a note of useful websites
items.example: During the workshop, make a note of useful websites for future reference.
items.note: Make a note of preserves information, rather than simply remembering it.

items.example: The old laptop may be infected with a virus.
items.note: The usual preposition after infected is with; this expression refers to malware on a device.

items.word: keep a copy of your work
items.pt: guardar uma cópia do seu trabalho
items.example: Always keep a copy of your work on a separate storage device.
items.note: A copy is a duplicate that can be used if the original is lost.

items.example: You can access your files from another device if the service is available.
items.note: Access is a transitive verb here; do not say access to your files when access is a verb.

items.word: have permission to view a file
items.pt: ter permissão para visualizar um arquivo
items.example: You must have permission to view a file in the shared folder.
items.note: Have permission to do something denotes authorisation, often managed by file settings.

units.title: Unit 28 — Study and learning
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 60–61 (PDF pages 64–65).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Work and study · education and academic communication
learningObjectives: Replace basic do and get expressions with natural academic verb–noun collocations while retaining their meaning.
Distinguish sitting or taking an exam from passing it, and do homework rather than make it.
Use suitable formal expressions for lectures, applications, assignments, qualifications and course withdrawal.
Discuss feedback, drafting, continuous assessment and further versus higher education in accurate English.

items.pt: prestar uma prova; fazer um exame
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Students will sit an exam at the end of the term.
items.note: Common especially in British English; sitting an exam does not mean passing it.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; prestar um exame
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: You must take an exam before entering the next level.
items.note: Take refers to participating in the exam; pass refers to a successful result.

items.pt: passar em uma prova; ser aprovado em um exame
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: You need to pass an exam to receive the qualification.
items.note: Pass means succeed, not merely take or sit the exam.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Our group will carry out research into renewable energy.
items.note: Carry out means perform a planned investigation; do research is also possible but less formal.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: The department plans to conduct research on reading habits.
items.note: Conduct research is a formal alternative to do research.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: We will carry out a research project over two semesters.
items.note: A research project is a specific organised study, often with a defined question and schedule.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: The students will conduct a research project on local transport.
items.note: Conduct emphasises directing and undertaking a planned investigation.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: I'd like to enrol on a course in technical writing.
items.note: Enrol on a course is a common British English pattern; enrol in a course is also common.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: She decided to take a course in digital electronics.
items.note: Take a course means study it; it does not necessarily mean finish it.

items.pt: estudar para obter um diploma universitário
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: My friend plans to study for a degree in biology.
items.note: Study for highlights working towards a qualification.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: He hopes to take a degree in mathematics at university.
items.note: In British English, take a degree can describe undertaking degree-level study; study for a degree is often clearer.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: I want to study history at university next year.
items.note: Study and take can replace informal do when describing an academic subject.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Students can take a subject outside their main degree programme.
items.note: Take a subject means choose and study it as part of a programme.

items.pt: escrever uma redação acadêmica; produzir um ensaio
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: We have to write an essay about climate policy.
items.note: Write an essay is more precise than do an essay.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: You must write an assignment based on the readings.
items.note: Write an assignment suits written coursework; assignments can also involve other activities.

items.pt: ministrar uma palestra ou aula expositiva
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: The visiting scientist will give a lecture on robotics.
items.note: Give a lecture is the normal teacher or speaker perspective; attend a lecture is the listener's.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: She will give a talk about her recent research.
items.note: Give a talk refers to presenting orally to an audience; it can be less formal than a lecture.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: You can obtain a diploma after completing the programme.
items.note: Obtain is a formal verb for receiving a qualification through study or assessment.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: To be awarded a diploma, candidates must complete all modules.
items.note: Be awarded emphasises formal conferral by an institution.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Students usually receive a grade after their assignments are marked.
items.note: Receive is more formal than get; a grade assesses performance.

items.pt: receber uma nota; ter uma nota atribuída
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Each student will be given a grade for the final project.
items.note: A passive alternative to receive a grade; the assessor assigns the result.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: You may need to obtain a qualification before applying for the position.
items.note: Obtain a qualification is a formal alternative to get a qualification.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: She hopes to acquire a qualification in accounting next year.
items.note: Acquire is formal and stresses gaining something through effort or training.

items.pt: receber educação formal; ter acesso à educação
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Every child should be able to receive an education.
items.note: Receive an education means have access to education or schooling.

items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Many programmes aim to help children receive a basic education.
items.note: Basic education refers to foundational schooling; receive fits the education context.

items.pt: fazer sua lição de casa; fazer a tarefa de casa
items.section: A · Alternatives to do and get
items.example: Remember to do your homework before the lesson.
items.note: Use do your homework, not make your homework.

items.pt: assistir a uma palestra ou aula expositiva
items.example: I will attend a lecture on digital communications tomorrow.
items.note: Attend is more formal than go to and takes no to before the event.

items.pt: comparecer a todas as aulas expositivas
items.example: You must attend all the lectures to complete this module.
items.note: Attend describes being present, not presenting the lecture.

items.example: You must complete a course before receiving the certificate.
items.note: Complete means finish the course successfully or fulfil all its requirements.

items.example: A class is held in the computer laboratory every Tuesday.
items.note: Hold is used in the passive to state when or where a class takes place.

items.example: Please hand in an essay at the end of the month.
items.note: Hand in means submit work to a teacher; it is a separable phrasal verb.

items.pt: apresentar uma candidatura; enviar uma inscrição formal
items.example: You must submit an application before the closing date.
items.note: Submit is formal and is natural for applications, documents and coursework.

items.example: Remember to submit your application before Friday.
items.note: The object follows submit directly; formal written submissions commonly take submit.

items.pt: desistir de um curso; cancelar a matrícula em um curso
items.example: You may withdraw from a course within the first two weeks.
items.note: Withdraw from is the formal pattern for leaving a course after enrolling.

items.pt: abandonar um curso; sair de um curso
items.example: Students who want to leave a course should contact the office.
items.note: Leave a course is more neutral and less formal than withdraw from a course.

items.example: You must hand in your essays before the final class.
items.note: Hand in is common for student work; essays is simply the plural form.

items.example: I keep a vocabulary notebook to review new expressions.
items.note: Keep here means maintain and use over time, not merely store the notebook.

items.example: It's helpful to record new collocations with example sentences.
items.note: Record means write down and organise language items for later study.

items.pt: um primeiro rascunho; uma primeira versão
items.example: I finished a first draft of my report last weekend.
items.note: A draft is an unfinished version that may be revised.

items.pt: uma versão final; um texto final revisado
items.example: She checked the citations before submitting a final draft.
items.note: The final draft is the revised version intended for submission.

items.example: Tutors often give feedback on students' writing.
items.note: Feedback is uncountable in this sense; say some feedback, not a feedback.

items.pt: receber retorno; receber comentários sobre o desempenho
items.example: You will receive feedback after the practical session.
items.note: Receive feedback describes getting comments that can help improvement.

items.example: Our course uses continuous assessment instead of one final exam.
items.note: Performance is evaluated through several tasks over time, rather than only a final test.

items.example: The college will provide training for new laboratory technicians.
items.note: Provide training is an institutional expression for offering instruction in practical skills.

items.example: Many people enter higher education after finishing secondary school.
items.note: Higher education refers to university-level or comparable post-secondary academic study.

items.example: The report examines access to tertiary education in rural areas.
items.note: Tertiary education is a formal alternative to higher education in many contexts.

items.pt: educação continuada; formação pós-secundária não universitária
items.example: He chose further education at a technical college rather than university.
items.note: In British English, further education typically means non-university post-secondary study or vocational courses; systems vary by country.

items.pt: curso de educação continuada ou profissionalizante
items.example: She enrolled on a further education course in electrical installation.
items.note: A course in further education may be academic or vocational but is normally outside a university degree.

items.example: Some employers recognise foreign qualifications after checking the documents.
items.note: Recognise means formally accept or acknowledge qualifications issued elsewhere.

items.pt: escola de ensino secundário; escola de ensino médio
items.example: Students often make important course choices during secondary school.
items.note: British English refers to schooling after primary school; exact age ranges vary by country.

items.pt: uma escola técnica; um instituto de formação técnica
items.example: He studied computer maintenance at a technical college.
items.note: Technical college refers to an institution providing practical or vocational programmes.

items.example: Before the exam, revise your notes on the key topics.
items.note: In British English revise often means study again for an exam; US English often uses review.

items.pt: diploma de bacharelado; graduação de bacharel
items.example: She completed a bachelor's degree in engineering last year.
items.note: A bachelor's degree is an undergraduate qualification; the possessive apostrophe is part of the term.

items.example: Many students prepare for school-leaving exams during their final year.
items.note: These are exams taken towards the end of school, with country-specific rules.

items.example: You need to get good grades to qualify for the scholarship.
items.note: Get good grades is ordinary spoken English; receive good grades is more formal.

items.pt: fornecer comentários sobre um trabalho escrito
items.example: Teachers usually give feedback on an essay after marking it.
items.note: Give feedback on identifies the work receiving comments.

items.example: Employers may recognise qualifications from accredited colleges.
items.note: Recognise refers to acknowledging the validity or standing of a qualification.

items.example: It helps to write words down in context rather than memorising isolated terms.
items.note: In context means recording examples showing how a word is naturally used.
